https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Van Gogh protest wants world’s ear on climate
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
Climate protesters glued themselves to the frame of a Van Gogh painting at Somerset House in London yesterday.
Visitors watched as two people from the Just Stop Oil group attached themselves to Peach Trees in Blossom, a 19th-century work in the Courtauld Gallery. The area around the painting was cordoned off by gallery staff during the protest and the museum was then closed.
A man and a woman were arrested for criminal damage, the Metropolitan Police said.
Just Stop Oil, which has protested at oil terminals and government offices, said it was calling for art institutions to join the group in “civil resistance” against climate change.
Just Stop Oil said that Provence, the region in southeastern France depicted in Peach Trees in Blossom, is “running desperately low on water” and may “soon be experiencing drought”.
The group shared on social media a picture of a man and woman in orange T-shirts attached to the painting’s frame.
One protester, Louis McKechnie, 21, from Weymouth, said: “As a kid I used to love this painting. My dad took me to see it when we visited London. I still love this painting, but I love my friends and family more, I love nature more.”
Another protester, Emily Brocklebank, 24, said: “Billionaires are getting richer while nurses queue at food banks, tens of millions of people across the world are starving and half the world’s population is exposed to extreme danger from heatwaves, floods, fires and famine. Meanwhile, the art establishment, the politicians and the fossil fuel companies look the other way.”
A spokesman for the Courtauld said the gallery would reopen to the public as normal today.
Five members of Just Stop Oil were arrested in Glasgow on Wednesday after they glued themselves to another 19th-century landscape painting in the city’s Kelvingrove Art Gallery.
They attached themselves to the frame of My Heart’s in the Highlands by the Scottish artist Horatio McCulloch and allegedly sprayed the group’s logo in orange paint on the walls and floor.

image.caption: Supporters of Just Stop Oil are stuck to the frame of Peach Trees in Blossom as police close in at London’s Courtauld Gallery

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/formula-o.title: British Grand Prix 2022: Zhou Guanyu miraculously unscathed after horror crash at Silverstone
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/formula-o.subtitle: Alfa Romeo escapes injury after multi-car incident on first corner
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/formula-o.text:
Alfa Romeo’s Zhou Guanyu miraculously escaped unharmed from a horrific crash at the British Grand Prix during a dramatic opening lap which also featured environmental activists invading the track.
At the first corner of an incident-packed race at Silverstone, which was won by Ferrari’s Carlos Sainz, Zhou, the 23-year-old Chinese driver, clipped George Russell’s Mercedes, flipped upside down and skidded off the track.
With its progress barely halted by the trackside gravel, the car flew over the tyre barrier before coming to rest, crumpled, against the perimeter fence. The race was red-flagged and, remarkably, Zhou was able to walk away from the wreck largely unharmed — saved by the halo head protection system. “What happened showed what a boon to safety halo is,” Max Verstappen, the reigning world champion, said.
Medical staff were quickly on the scene to remove Zhou from the car before he was taken by ambulance to the medical centre. Forty minutes later, race control announced that the Alfa Romeo driver, in his first Formula One season, was “conscious and talking”, adding: “There are no fractures and considering the circumstances he’s pretty good.” Zhou later tweeted a picture of himself and confirmed that he was feeling “OK”.
Amid the chaos of turn one, Aston Martin’s Sebastian Vettel also rammed Alexander Albon, of Williams, who crashed into the barrier and was taken to hospital as a precaution. Russell was also ruled out of the rest of race because he needed assistance to restart his car.
Sainz, who went on to register his first F1 win at the 150th attempt, said of Zhou: “I wasn’t very happy to see him taken away like that, but when I saw the crash later, I was completely shocked. It was incredible. The fact he came out of it is crazy.”
Earlier in the day, in Formula Two, Dennis Hauger’s car landed on top of Roy Nissany, who was also saved by his halo — the cockpit protection device which sits above the driver’s head, introduced to top-level motorsport in 2018. “Today, the FIA has saved two lives,” Sainz added. “You guys cannot imagine the speed we are doing, changing direction, and knowing we can do it safely. I thank them for this, and I love the sport for that.”
Sergio Pérez, who finished second for Red Bull, added: “It’s been a while since there’s been an accident like that. You have to eliminate it from your mind and focus on what you have to do.”
McLaren’s Daniel Ricciardo said he could not bear to watch any replays of the incident before the race restarted.
“I saw where he flipped over out of the corner of my eye,” Ricciardo said. “But once I knew he was OK, I chose not to watch it. You have to think of other things when you have a ten-minute warning before the restart.
“I’ll watch the replays tonight and then try to understand it. The fact he got out is a massive positive. Double thumbs up for the halo, that’s a big plus.”
The crash potentially averted another catastrophe. As the red flag was raised and the remaining drivers slowed down on their way back to the pit lane, seven protesters from the environmental group Just Stop Oil ran onto the track and sat down.
The group, which campaigns for an immediate end to new fossil-fuel investments — often by disrupting large-scale public events — tweeted: “If you are more outraged about this disruption than our world being burnt before our eyes, then you need to get your priorities straight.”
Northamptonshire police had tweeted on Saturday night that they had intelligence which predicted the incursion. That information had not been passed on to Ricciardo, who saw the protesters from his cockpit.
“The police? I had no idea,” the Australian said. “That said, I don’t know if it would change anything for us. We’re good enough to slow down.”
After the race, there was surprise when Lewis Hamilton, who finished third, showed his support for the climate activists.
Northamptonshire Police said seven people had been arrested. Five had managed to get onto the Wellington Straight — the fastest point of the track — before sitting down. The race had already been suspended after Zhou’s crash, but a number of cars sped by as the protesters, understood to be from the climate activist group Just Stop Oil, launched their action.
They were dragged away by marshals to huge cheers from the watching crowd. But later Hamilton declared: “Big up those guys. Big up the protesters. I love that people are fighting for the planet and we need more people like them.”
Mercedes later put out a statement, which said: “Lewis was endorsing their right to protest but not the method that they chose, which compromised their safety and that of others.” The seven-times world champion also sought to clarify his comments in an Instagram post. “Please don’t jump on to our race circuits to protest, we don’t want to put you in harm’s way,” he wrote.
Sainz agreed. “I support the cause,” he said, “but I don’t believe jumping on to an F1 track is the right way to do it. You could kill them.”
The race was restarted after a delay of almost an hour without Zhou, Albon or Russell, who — having left his car to check on Zhou — unsuccessfully appealed at some length to be reinstated. “When I got back to my car I couldn’t restart it,” Russell said. “As soon as you get assistance you can’t restart. It’s very frustrating as the car just had a puncture.
“The FIA are pretty adamant — it’s one of those unique scenarios I guess.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insi.title: Inside Jack Harries and Alice Aedy’s pad in Hackney, east London
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/insi.text:
Sweden has Greta Thunberg, Britain has Jack Harries. The documentary film-maker and climate activist, 29, is the Harry Styles of the environmental movement: he has interviewed Barack Obama and Sir David Attenborough, and amassed 1.3 million followers on Instagram and 3.7 million subscribers on YouTube, with beautifully shot films of Earth in peril. Yet some of the user comments are less about carbon footprints and more about his looks: “Whaddababe”; “Sexy eco-warrior” etc.
“The internet rewards a certain type of thing. And so I think we play that game in order to further the message we’re passionate about,” says Harries, on a Zoom chat from his newly renovated loft-style flat in a 1920s former shoe factory flat in Hackney, east London, where he lives with his girlfriend, Alice Aedy, 27, also a photographer and film-maker.
That message is to raise awareness of climate change through storytelling. In 2020 Aedy, Harries and his twin brother, Finn, established a production company, Earthrise Studio, that produces films and photojournalism about communities on the front lines of global warming — in Kiribati, Somaliland, Greenland, Bhutan, Borneo. “We spent a few years going on Extinction Rebellion protests but our friends and families didn’t want to go on the marches; it all felt a bit extreme,” he says. “We wanted to find a way to bridge the gap . . . and try to change the perception of what it is to be an environmentalist. [When I was] growing up, it was a hippy with long hair and candles and no one wants to sort of join that movement. We’re trying to frame it to be a little bit more aspirational.”
Their home and activist HQ certainly fits that dream — there are no tie-dye prints, wind chimes and hair shirts here. The couple, who met five and a half years ago when they were working in the Jungle refugee camp in Calais, dreamt of creating a live/work space with good light where they could shoot stills and video, and record podcasts. It’s a far cry from making YouTube videos in his bedroom. Harries rose to fame when he was 18, when he and Finn made fun, wacky videos in their gap year (making his bedroom into a ball pit; blowing up pumpkins). They became so successful that in 2011, when Google emailed him to say that he could monetise his content, Harries quit university after only one term at Bristol. “My parents were horrified.” (He has since gained a master’s degree from University College London in documentary film-making.)
The 1,000 sq ft space was renovated by the architect Studio McW. Aedy’s brief was “a multipurpose live/work space. We wanted to celebrate the materiality of the space: the concrete and brick, lots of joinery, and add clay to the walls for a textural, earthy feel.” The flat is two storeys, with an upside-down layout: the living space upstairs and the bedroom downstairs. The original layout was odd: the front door opened right into the bedroom (they have since built a little corridor). Upstairs they knocked down walls to create a vast open-plan space. The result is London’s coolest WFH pad, with high ceilings, roof lights, exposed beams, handcrafted joinery, a long table, Sage coffee maker and a chillout zone — Earthrise Studio’s team of seven congregates here for brainstorming sessions. Open plan is noisy, however. Aedy says: “In hindsight, maybe we would have done things differently.”
Aedy’s original vision was a “hyper-minimalist” space, but it quickly turned into a jungle thanks to their lockdown love affair with the houseplant delivery website Patch Plants. “We don’t really see a plant out of our window so we’ve had to bring nature in,” Aedy says.
The new staircase is made from reclaimed timber; the clay walls are by a Cornish company called Clayworks and apparently absorb toxins. The couple have an almost vegan diet (they eat eggs) and are upgrading their Crittall-style windows to double-glazing, but admit they are not saints. They had concrete worktops made during the renovation. “It is sturdy but I don’t know if we would do it again; we don’t love the environmental impact of concrete and it does stain,” Aedy says.
“We’re aware of that conversation around hypocrisy and we try to be really honest and say, we are far from perfect,” she adds. Aedy says that they do carbon offsets when they fly, donate to the communities where they film and try to use remote film crews on projects rather than flying there. “This is about creating systems and structures that allow us all to do better rather than pointing a finger at the individual.”
When they’re not on assignment they’re living the young east London dream. They run around Victoria Park, swim at London Fields Lido and buy their coffee beans from Broadway Market. “It took me a while to convince Jack to move to east London,” Aedy says. “But within about 24 hours he was going to the E5 Bakehouse, getting the loaf of bread in the morning on his very east London bike. And I just thought, ‘This guy’s happy.’ ”
When they go out for coffee it’s to La Bouche on Broadway Market. “We always wanted a regular coffee place, where they know your order, just like in Friends,” Aedy says.
With millions of followers on social media, Harries does get recognised. “There were a couple of years where it was quite mental. Interactions on the street were quite overwhelming — screaming and that sort of thing,” he says, although he is trying to shift the focus away from his image to the issues. “But as we’ve grown our audience have grown up as well. So people might now come up and say they’ve been studying environmental science and that’s really lovely because you can have much more nourishing conversations.”
Harries has spoken extensively about mental health, particularly the issue of climate anxiety. Can he offer any hope? “I’ve lost a lot of hope in top-down change,” he says. “I’ve found my hope is in people who take action in their own communities. I met a young woman called Poppy Okotcha in Totnes [in Devon] who turned her normal garden into an abundant rewilded vegetable garden, and a guy called Ryan in the Orkneys who works on a tidal turbine that creates energy. He said to me, ‘Instead of people getting arrested on the streets, why don’t they just get on with it and do things?’ That’s an example of a community that became self-reliant in terms of energy. I think that’s where the hope lies.”earthrise.studio; studiomcw.co.uk

https://www.thetimes.com/article/get-tou.title: Get tough with fuel protesters, police told
https://www.thetimes.com/article/get-tou.subtitle: Fears of summer gridlock if campaign spreads
https://www.thetimes.com/article/get-tou.text:
Police have been urged to take a zero-tolerance approach to fuel campaigners amid fears that “go-slow” protests on motorways could continue throughout the summer.
Senior government sources said Priti Patel, the home secretary, expected forces to use new powers to prevent a repeat of yesterday, when convoys of protesters brought parts of the road network to a standstill.
The action mainly targeted motorways, with vehicles crawling at below 30mph along two lanes, leaving the outside lane free. Among roads affected were the M4 and Prince of Wales bridge over the River Severn, the M5 in Devon, the M32, the A38, the M180 in Lincolnshire, the A12 in Essex, the A92 in Scotland and the A64 near York.
• Leading article: The government needs to explain why the cost of the Ukraine war is worth paying
Police made 13 arrests during the demonstrations, which were coordinated by Fuel Price Stand Against Tax — a new group protesting against record fuel costs. Unlike groups such as Insulate Britain or Just Stop Oil, they are not motivated by a green agenda.
Campaigners have warned that protests will continue if the government does not do more to address fuel prices. Petrol has risen from 145p to 191.5p a litre since the start of the year, with about 45 per cent of the cost now made up of VAT and fuel duty.
Patel’s stance was backed by Downing Street, which said the prime minister expected the police to take firm action under the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act to ensure that the road network did not grind to a halt as a consequence of go-slow protests.
“The government has given the police a lot of powers to deal with this sort of stuff and we are looking to them to use it,” a senior government source said. “We want to know what they are going to do about it.”
The Home Office highlighted new powers in the policing act, which was given royal assent in April, that increased the maximum penalty for blocking a highway to six months’ imprisonment and an unlimited fine.
The offence was primarily introduced to deal with direct action environmental campaigns but ministers believe police should also apply it to petrol protests.
“The last thing we want to see is these kinds of protests continuing and disrupting people’s travel plans over the summer. We expect the police to enforce the law,” the source said.
“Through our Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act, we have given the police a wealth of powers to deal with disruptive and damaging protests, including imprisonment and unlimited fines for those blocking a highway — actions which inflict further pain on those affected by rising prices. The home secretary would encourage and support the police to make use of all the powers available to them.”
A government source said that police had seemed more concerned with pulling over a driver who had used a motorway hard shoulder to “undertake” vehicles going slowly on the main carriageway than with tackling the action’s ringleaders. They also suggested that police should immediately prosecute any protesters who had filmed themselves driving.
“That should be an immediate six points on their licence and we would expect the police to pursue that,” the source added.
Downing Street and the Treasury have not ruled out further cuts to fuel duty in addition to the 5p cut brought in this year. However, they said any announcement would have to wait until the autumn budget and would depend on the wholesale price of oil later in the year.
It is feared in government that the protests will be the start of a new movement akin to the gilets jaunes in France, the grassroots yellow-vest protesters who campaign for economic justice.
FairFuelUK, which is urging the government to reduce fuel duty by at least 20p, warned that the demonstrations would worsen if the cost does not come down. Howard Cox, the founder of FairFuelUK, said that other European countries, such as Germany, Spain and France, had introduced substantial cuts to fuel duty and questioned why the UK government was not going beyond the 5p cut announced in March.
He added: “I wasn’t involved in setting these protests up but I do support them provided they’re lawful, because these drivers, truckers and white-van men are reaching the absolute end of their tether with the current levels of prices at the pumps.”
The Facebook page advertising the event called for people to take their cars, lorries and tractors to cause roadblocks all over the country “until there is change”.
Richard Dite, 44, a mobile welder from Maesteg, south Wales, was filmed leading the M4 procession in his van shortly after he blasted the Pirates of the Caribbean theme tune with his horn.
Before the protest started he said that it was costing him hundreds of pounds to get to work every week because of the rising price of fuel.
“It’s costing me £300 a week before I even get to work and earn anything,” he said. “My only option soon will be to put the welding gear in the shed and call it a day, maybe go on the dole. Face it, at this rate I’ll be on more that way.”
Vicky Stamper, from Cwmbran, south Wales, decided to take part after she and her husband Darren had to give up their jobs in Bristol because they could no longer afford to commute.
Stamper, 41, a former HGV driver who was arrested during the protest, said: “We had to leave those jobs because it was costing us £380 a week just to get to and from work.
“I then lost a job two weeks ago because the company couldn’t afford to put fuel in that many lorries — so last in, first out.” Stamper said that the situation had taken an emotional toll on her and her family.
Talking before the protest about the disruption that would be caused to drivers, Stamper said: “We’re doing this for us and for them.
“If they want to have a moan, they should join us instead.” When asked what she would ask prime minister Boris Johnson to do, she said: “Resign.”
Another of the protest organisers on the M4 was a mechanic named Pickle Doherty, 36, whose business is registered in Basingstoke, Hampshire. He told The Daily Telegraph that the cost of diesel is “ripping me apart” as he travels to customers, covering up to 80 miles a day. “Sooner or later my radius will be smaller, leaving less chance of work. That’s why I felt the need to do this.”
The RAC’s fuel spokesman, Simon Williams, said there did not appear to be any sign of retailers reducing forecourt prices, even though weekly wholesale costs had fallen for five weeks.
Gordon Balmer, executive director of the Petrol Retailers Association, which represents independent forecourts, said that rising wholesale prices were related to international events and the weakness of the pound against the US dollar.
Rishi Sunak, the chancellor, has said that he will carefully consider calls for a “more substantial” fuel duty cut after the 5p per litre reduction failed to halt price rises.
Rising fuel prices have been pushed even higher by the war in Ukraine, with Russia, one of the world’s largest oil exporters, facing sanctions.
The government has said that although it understands people are struggling with rising prices and have a right to protest, “people’s day to day lives should not be disrupted” and warned that traffic delays “will only add to fuel use”.
A National Police Chiefs’ Council spokesman said: “The ability to protest peacefully in a democracy is important but it is also important there are consequences for those who break the law. We will take necessary action against anyone who chooses to act outside the law. Police are trained to strict national standards and officers are able to deal with a wide range of tactics being deployed by protesters.”

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Just Stop Oil protesters glue themselves to Constable’s Hay Wain at National Gallery
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.subtitle: Protesters also covered the painting with a ‘dystopian’ version of the scene
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
Climate activists have glued themselves to one of Britain’s best-known works of art after masking it with a different image in a protest at the National Gallery.
Just Stop Oil protesters attached themselves to the frame of The Hay Wain, by John Constable, and overlaid the painting with a “reimagined” dystopian vision of the scene.
The artwork, completed in 1821, shows an idyllic vision of the millpond at Flatford on the River Stour in Suffolk. According to the group, the new print “depicts a nightmare scene that demonstrates how oil will destroy our countryside”.
“The river has gone ... replaced by a road,” a spokesman said. “Planes fill the sky, pollution belches from cities on the horizon, trees are scorched by wildfires, an old car is dumped in front of the mill and the famous hay wain cart carries an old washing machine.”
Just Stop Oil are calling on the government to end new oil and gas facilities and for art institutions to join their group in civil resistance.
Hannah Hunt, 23, a psychology student from Brighton, said: “I’m here because our government plans to license 40 new UK oil and gas projects in the next few years. This makes them complicit in pushing the world towards an unliveable climate, and in the deaths of billions of people in the coming decades.”
Eben Lazarus, 22, a music student from Brighton, said: “I support Just Stop Oil’s demand for our government to halt all new oil and gas projects in the UK immediately. I want to work in the arts, not disrupt them, but the situation we’re in means we must do everything we peacefully can to prevent the total collapse of our ordered society.
“I have a number of younger siblings, the youngest are just 10 and 12, and I refuse to stand and watch them being condemned to a future of suffering. Our government is failing in its fundamental duty to protect us.
“We have covered The Hay Wain with a reimagined version that illustrates the expected impact of our addiction to fossil fuels on our countryside. The painting is an important part of our heritage, but it is not more important than the 3.5 billion men, women and children already in danger because of the climate crisis.”
On Sunday protesters ran on to the track at Silverstone during the British Grand Prix, after an opening-lap crash involving the Alfa Romeo driver Zhou Guanyu. Seven people were arrested and Just Stop Oil claimed responsibility.
After the race Lewis Hamilton, who finished third, showed his support for the activists, who were dragged away by marshals to huge cheers from the watching crowd. “Big up those guys,” he said. “Big up the protesters. I love that people are fighting for the planet and we need more people like them.”
The National Gallery said that the painting had been removed to be examined by the conservation team. “The Hay Wain suffered minor damage to its frame and there was also some disruption to the surface of the varnish on the painting, both of which have now been successfully dealt with,” it said. “The painting will be rehung in Room 34, ready for when the National Gallery opens at 10am on Tuesday, July 5.’
In 2013 The Hay Wain was attacked by a Fathers4Justice protester who glued a four-inch photo of a young boy to it but did no lasting damage.

image.caption: Just Stop Oil activists masked The Hay Wain, gluing their hands to its frameTOM BOWLES/STORY PICTURE AGENCY

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Just Stop Oil protesters glue themselves to Last Supper at the Royal Academy
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
Climate activists have glued themselves to the frame of a copy of Leonardo da Vinci’s The Last Supper at the Royal Academy in London.
The five activists stuck their hands to the frame of Giampietrino’s full-scale copy of the famous work and sprayed “no new oil” across the wall below it. Just Stop Oil campaigners said yesterday’s actions were “the fifth time in the past week that supporters of the group had disrupted a major art institution in an act of civil resistance”. On Monday, two people were arrested after protesters attached themselves to the frame of The Hay Wain, by John Constable, at the National Gallery and overlaid the painting with a dystopian vision of the scene.
Just Stop Oil wants ministers to halt new oil and gas licences in the UK and for directors, staff and members of art institutions to join their cause. Lucy Porter, 47, a former primary school teacher and climate activist from Leeds, said: “When I was teaching I brought my students to great institutions like the Royal Academy. But now it feels unfair to expect them to respect our culture when their government is hellbent on destroying their future by licensing new oil and gas projects.”
Last Friday at Manchester Art Gallery, two supporters glued themselves to the frame of Thomson’s Aeolian Harp (1809) by JMW Turner, a painting of a view overlooking the Thames from Richmond Hill. The Vincent Van Gogh painting Peach Trees in Blossom (1889) was targeted on June 30 at the Courtauld Gallery in London. One activist said: “I’m not willing to be marched to my death by the fossil fuel companies and their government puppets.”
At Kelvingrove art gallery and museum in Glasgow last Wednesday, three protesters sprayed paint around a 19th-century landscape by Horatio McCulloch called My Heart’s in the Highlands, and two glued themselves to the frame. Hannah Torrance Bright, 20, a student from the Glasgow School of Art, said: “You should be outraged at this action — I’m outraged because I feel I have no choice but to resist the government’s genocidal plans.”
While big oil is deeply embedded within Britain’s cultural institutions, the galleries targeted this week by climate change activists are not those that have taken the “fossil fuel shilling” (David Sanderson writes).
So why have protesters not glued themselves to a segment of Parthenon marble at the British Museum, which has just launched another exhibition with BP as the main sponsor?
“It is not about fossil fuel sponsorship this time,” said Mel Carrington, a spokeswoman for Just Stop Oil. “It is the whole shooting match.”
All institutions need to wake up and “resist”, she said — because there will be no point in art after climate change-induced “genocide”.
Carrington added: “Art institutions need to step up. They need to be a force for good.”
